statement: A net is made of 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. It folds up into a closed solid with no gaps or overlaps. How many edges does the solid have?

choices.misconception: I counted the sides around the outside of the flat net, but two outside sides join up to make one edge.
I counted the 3 sides of each triangle and then 2 long sides of each rectangle, so each long edge shared by two rectangles was counted twice.
I counted all 18 sides of the pieces and took away only the 4 fold lines, as if the other sides did not pair up.
I counted every side of every piece, but each edge of the solid is where two sides meet.

hints: Count the sides of all five pieces together.
When the net folds up, every edge of the solid is made by two sides of the pieces meeting. Count all the sides first, then allow for that pairing.
The pieces have 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 18 sides altogether. Each edge uses two of them.

solutions.reliable: The solid is a triangular prism: two triangle ends joined by three rectangles. The two triangles give 3 + 3 = 6 edges, and three long edges run between their corners, giving 9 edges in all. The transferable idea: every edge of a closed solid is shared by exactly two faces, which lets you count edges from the flat pieces.
solutions.elegant: The pieces have 2 x 3 + 3 x 4 = 18 sides. Every edge of the closed solid is shared by exactly two faces, so there are 18 / 2 = 9 edges, without needing to picture the solid at all.

whyOnTest: Nets test whether you can see flat pieces becoming a solid, and halving the total number of sides is a reliable way to count edges.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
